SCA/17262/2011 7/ 7 ORDER 
 
 

 

 

IN
THE HIGH COURT OF GUJARAT AT AHMEDABAD
 

 


 

SPECIAL
CIVIL APPLICATION No. 17262 of 2011
 

 
 
=========================================================


 

WOLSON
VISHVAS HARRY - Petitioner(s)
 

Versus
 

ANJALI
, D/O BABUBHAI PANDAV - Respondent(s)
 

=========================================================
 
Appearance : 
MR
MAKBUL I MANSURI for
Petitioner(s) : 1, 
MRCRMISHRA for Respondent(s) :
1, 
=========================================================


 
 
 
 
 
 

CORAM
 : 
 
 
 
 

HONOURABLE
 MS JUSTICE SONIA GOKANI
 
 

 

 
 


 

Date
: 24/04/2012 

 

 
 
ORAL
ORDER

1. This
petition is preferred challenging the order of the Family Court
passed below Exhibit 9 in Family Suit No. 1529 of 2009 dated 30th
July 2011.

1.1 To
briefly state the facts : The petitioner herein is the original
applicant before the Family Court who preferred Family Suit under
 section 32 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 for restitution of
conjugal rights. It is the say of the petitioner that he married the
respondent original opponent on 6th June 2002 as per the 
Christian Rites and Rituals and two children were begotten of the
said wedlock. On 6th September 2009 the respondent alleged
to have left the home of the petitioner and started living with her
step mother at Himmatnagar. She also never cared for the children 
and therefore notice was issued in the month of November 2009 asking
the respondent to fulfill her obligation of conjugal rights. Reply
to which was received and thereafter the said suit was filed being
Family Suit No.1529/2009.

2. An
application was preferred by the respondent vide Exh. 9 for alimony
as well as for expenses. An application under section 125 of the
Criminal Procedure Code for maintenance was also preferred being
Criminal Misc. Application NO. 1555/2010.

3. The
petitioner since decided not to pursue the proceedings of the Family
Suit a purshis was filed for withdrawal of the said suit which was
accepted with a noting "recorded" however, to the dismay 
of the petitioner the Court granted application preferred by the
respondent and directed the petitioner to pay the amount of Rs
1,500/- per month to the respondent and Rs 1,000/- to both the
children vide its order dated 22nd April 2010 as also a
sum of Rs 2000/- to legal expenses and Rs 200 towards lodging and
boarding charges for every adjournment when the respondent visited 
the Family Court.

3.1 On
18th October 2011 when the petitioner learnt about such
order and certified copy was asked for and this petition has been
preferred challenging the legality, propriety and reasonableness of
such an order.

4.
 Learned advocate Mr. Mansuri appearing for the petitioner
fervently urged that Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act would never
apply to the case of the present petitioner and therefore the Court
had wrongly applied the provisions of Section 24 of the Hindu
Marriage Act and therefore, the entire order is to be quashed. He
further urged that such an order could not have been passed when the
petitioner had chosen to withdraw the petition for restitution of
conjugal rights.

5. 
A purshis preferred by Exh. 12 has also been pressed into service
to point out that Court at an initial stage had recorded such a
purshis and kept the matter for hearing. And , thereafter further
order was passed.: "Today applicant is absent and this purshis 
not recorded". The order has been passed on 30th
July 2011. It also appears that certified copy when was obtained
on 18th October 2011 the Court has merely endorsed
"recorded" on purshis by passing order below Exh. 12.
However, subsequently on 25th November 2011 the order as
mentioned hereinabove has been passed.

5.1 The
Court once having recorded the purshis could have passed a
further order instead of erasing such order at a later date. During
the pendency of any application for interim alimony, any withdrawal
could not have been permitted by simply recording the same. The
possibility cannot be ruled out that on having realised such a
mistake, the Court chose to decide the application on merit which
was pending as having been earlier referred by respondent wife vide
Exh. 9. It in fact was necessary for the Court to decide an
application on merit as withdrawal of petition by the husband
possibly was with a view to defeat the right of interim alimony
asked for by the respondent wife, and the same cannot be endorsed by
the Court by giving such a permission without deciding the
request of interim alimony. Therefore, the Court is procedurally not
in error in reviewing its own earlier order. However such an action
 ought to have been put to the notice of the both the sides. At the
same time, it can be noticed from the record that withdrawal of
such petition during the pendency of an application for alimony
appear to be an attempt to overeach the Court's process.

6. Be
that as it may, specific question that has been raised by the
petitioner is granted as interim alimony pendentlite under section
24 of the Hindu Marriage Act when in fact the petition was
preferred under the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 .

6.1 It
can be noted from the record that the order under challenge passed
below Exh. 9 is in fact the application preferred under section 36 
of the Indian Divorce Act for interim alimony as well as the for
the expenses. This application preferred by the wife is for the
relief of grant of alimony of Rs 5,000/ per month with further
request of legal expenses of Rs 10,000/- and Rs 1,000/- for
attending to the court at Himmatnagar on every adjournment. She had
averred that the applicant is serving in the V.S Hospital and is
earning sum of Rs 15,000 to 20,000/- per month.

7. The
Court after a detailed discussion of circumstances existing on
the record as also considering the documentary evidences produced in
support of version of the respondent wife in respect of salary of the
petitioner concluded that she is entitled to the sum of Rs 1, 500/-
every month towards her maintenance pendent lite with Rs 2000/-
towards legal expenses and Rs 200 towards lodging and boarding 
charges for attending the Court on every adjournment. It is further
clarified that amount of interim maintenance granted should be
adjusted with the amount of maintenance awarded under section 125
of the criminal Procedure Code.

8. Learned
advocate for the petitioner urges this court that the Court had 
 Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act in mind all the time and
therefore, the order is ex facie, illegal and requires quashment
whereas learned advocate Mr. Gupta appearing for the wife urged
that Section 36 of the Hindu Divorce Act permits alimony pendent
lite in a suit and the wife also can present the petition for
expenses of the petition. He further urged that mere wrong mention
of provision would not take away the substance of the order.
 However, he admitted the maintenance granted to the children of Rs
1000/- each is wrongly awarded as both the children are with the
husband.

9. There
appears to be two errors evident in the order impugned firstly, 
the grant of maintenance pendent lite to both the children Rs 1000/-
per month when in fact admittedly the children are not with the
respondent wife therefore, to that extent, the order requires 
quashment.

9.1 Secondly,
the Court concerned while discussing issues before it instead of
referring to Section 36 in the operative portion of the order, it
made mention of Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act. This
apparently is an error however, as rightly pointed out by learned
advocate Mr. Sharma that mere wrong quoting of the provision cannot
provide the ground for this Court to sustain the version of the
petitioner and invoke supervisory jurisdiction to quash and set
aside the entire order which infact discussed all pros and cons and 
has awarded maintenance pendent lite. Therefore also invocation of
supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 would not be necessary 
for quashing the entire order.

10. 
 Section 36 of the Indian Divorce Act clearly provides alimony 
pendent lite. In a suit under this Act, whether instituted by 
husband or wife, the Court on being satisfied about the truth of
the statement contained in the petition, has a discretion of making 
any order on the husband, for the payment to the wife for
expenses of proceedings and alimony pending the suit as may deem
appropriate and just to the Court.

11. The
provision also stipulates the disposal of such petition within 60
days of the service of the husband. Thus, not only the Act provide
for interim alimony pendent lite, but, it also expects the Court 
to act provided within a time frame to ensure that the wife is not
left in a destitute condition.

12. As
can be noted from the plaint the same was preferred on 29th
December 2009 and an application for interim alimony was preferred 
on 22nd April 2010. Therefore, statutorily also, the Court
was required to decide the same within six months ie on or before 
22nd October 2010. Although, it was not decided 
during the said period and on 4th February 2011, the
husband petitioner herein chose to withdraw the petition of
divorce. The Court could not have permitted the same without
deciding the application of maintainance which it was required to 
 adjudicate within stipulated period as mentioned hereinabove 
however, there is no error in the Court deciding such application
after the said purshis of withdrawal was tendered. Neither on
procedurality nor in substance, the order impugned can be found
faulty, much less on the ground of causing deep prejudice to the
petitioner that the interference is warranted.

11. In
the light of the above discussion, the order is partly quashed.
Order of grant of maintainanance to both the children is hereby
quashed and technical defect of wrong reference of Section 24 of the
Hindu Marriage Act twice in the operative order stands corrected and
be read as section 36 of the Hindu Marriage Act.

12. This
petition stands disposed of in the above terms.

(Ms.
Sonia Gokani,J.)
